name: Evergreen
lede: Evergreen is a dark forest green named for trees that keep their leaves, recorded in color dictionaries since 1915.

sections.title: A tree word
sections.body: As a plain word, *evergreen* describes shrubs and trees whose foliage stays green through the year [1]. As a color, Paterson defines it as a yellowish green, and notes that Washington is called the Evergreen State [1]. The swatch is darker and bluer than that definition: the library reads it at lightness 26, chroma 30 and hue 156 in LCH, a dark green, not a yellowish one [2]. Books disagree with the swatch, then, about the hue.

sections.title: The record in the color lists
sections.body: Evergreen is in the xkcd survey, the 1955 ISCC-NBS system (block 137), and the Maerz & Paul dictionary, which gives first use as 1915 on plate 24 E 12 [2]. The ISCC-NBS lists give the same block the names Amarna (first use 1923), Dark Emerald Green, Deep Emerald Green and Service Corps [2]. British Racing Green and UP Forest Green are near-duplicates, about 2 in ΔE away [2]. St Clair describes racing green as a dark evergreen associated with early British car racing [3]. The nearest named color is [[hunter-green]], 8.8 apart [2]; [[forest-green]] and [[racing-green]] are close company.

sections.title: Evergreens in the books
sections.body: The books know evergreens mostly as plants. Finlay notes that the pine, being evergreen, often symbolizes eternal life, and links it with the goddess Cybele [4]. Linnaeus urged Swedes to drink a tea of *Linnaea borealis*, an evergreen shrub, though his own son admitted it could be rather repulsive [5]. Two more colorants come from evergreens: the yellow resin gamboge from Southeast Asian trees, and annatto, a yellow to red-orange dye from the seeds of the shrub *Bixa orellana* [6][7].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The xkcd list gives a second hex for the name, #05480D, which is a little more yellow-green and agrees better with Paterson's wording [2]. Screen colors are approximate.
